summary: Learners build the reactivity series of common metals (potassium down to gold) from observed evidence rather than memorising a mnemonic, then use positions in the series to predict displacement reactions and to explain why carbon can extract some metals (iron) but not others (aluminium, which needs electrolysis). Representation stays at the word-equation, qualitative level appropriate for ages 12–14; electrode half-equations and quantitative electrolysis are deferred to later study.
misconceptions: Treating the series as an arbitrary list to memorise rather than an ordering by measurable reactivity.
Thinking any metal can displace any other, rather than only a more reactive metal displacing a less reactive one.
Believing carbon can extract all metals, missing that metals above carbon (e.g. aluminium) need electrolysis.
Confusing 'reactive' with 'strong' or 'heavy' — assuming gold or iron must be very reactive because they are hard or dense.
Assuming the deposited copper in a displacement reaction is a coating of the original metal rather than newly formed copper metal.

activities.title: Rank the metals by observed vigour
steps: Observe each of several metals reacting with water and, separately, with dilute acid, recording what happens: fizzing rate, bubbles, any temperature rise, whether anything happens at all. The most reactive metals (potassium, sodium) are never handled by learners: their reactions with water are shown by simulation or teacher demonstration only, and their reactions with acid are far too violent to demonstrate, so these are shown by simulation only. Safer metals (e.g. magnesium, zinc, iron, copper) can be tested hands-on where feasible.

Use the observations to arrange the metals into an ordered list from most reactive to least reactive. For example, note from the demonstration/simulation that potassium reacts violently, that magnesium fizzes strongly in acid, and that copper shows essentially no reaction.
Mark where carbon and hydrogen sit as reference points once the metal order is established from the evidence.
Write a short justification for the placement of two chosen metals, citing the specific observation (e.g. 'magnesium is above zinc because it fizzed faster in the same acid').
activities.insight: The reactivity series is an ordering by measurable reactivity — how vigorously a metal reacts with water and acid — not an arbitrary list to recite. Position reflects evidence.

activities.title: Displacement grid — more reactive pushes out less reactive
steps: Lower each metal strip (e.g. iron nail, zinc, magnesium, copper) into each of several metal-salt solutions (e.g. copper sulfate, magnesium sulfate, zinc sulfate) and record which pairings react and which do nothing.
Observe the tell-tale signs of displacement: an iron nail in blue copper sulfate grows an orange copper coating while the blue colour fades.
For each cell of the grid, state before testing whether you expect a reaction based on the series, then compare with what happens.
Write the word equation for a reaction that occurred, e.g. iron + copper sulfate → iron sulfate + copper.
Explain whether the orange solid on the nail is the original metal or newly formed copper.
activities.insight: A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one from its compound, and the reaction runs only one way. The deposited metal (e.g. copper) is newly formed, not a transferred coating of the original metal.

activities.title: Extraction bench — why carbon works for iron but not aluminium
steps: Watch a teacher demonstration or simulation of heating a metal oxide with carbon and record the result: iron oxide is reduced to iron, while aluminium oxide is not reduced. (This is a high-temperature reaction, so it is demonstrated or simulated, not run hands-on by learners.)
Locate carbon's position in the series and identify which metal oxides lie below it (can be reduced by carbon) and which lie above it (cannot).
State the method needed to extract aluminium (electrolysis) and explain why carbon alone is not enough.

Build a short timeline linking extraction difficulty to history: gold found native (unreactive), iron smelted with carbon since antiquity, aluminium first isolated only in the 1820s (using an even more reactive metal, not carbon) and made cheaply in bulk only after industrial electrolysis began in the 1880s.
Explain the direction of cause and effect: gold is found as pure nuggets because it is unreactive — its rarity does not cause its low reactivity.
activities.insight: Carbon can reduce oxides of metals below it in the series (e.g. iron) but not those above it (e.g. aluminium), which require electrolysis. Reactivity causes the extraction difficulty and the historical timeline, not the other way round.

activities.title: Predict–Observe–Explain: the paired beakers
steps: Before anything is mixed, look at two setups: a strip of magnesium going into blue copper sulfate, and a strip of copper going into colourless magnesium sulfate. Predict which one reacts and WHY.
Commit your reasoning in writing before observing — this prediction is the point of the task.
Observe: only the magnesium-in-copper-sulfate reacts (blue fades, copper deposits on the strip); copper in magnesium sulfate does nothing.
Explain the result using reactivity order, then extend: if magnesium displaces zinc and zinc displaces iron, predict what magnesium does to iron sulfate and how confident you are.
Answer the challenge: why won't ranking metals by how heavy they are predict displacement?
activities.insight: Ordering metals by reactivity predicts exactly one reaction and names its direction. A model based on 'stronger/heavier/tougher wins' or 'any two metals react' mispredicts. The reasoning, not just the observation, shows understanding.

activities.title: Reactivity ladder reference with history cards
steps: Consult a labelled vertical reactivity ladder from potassium (top) to gold (bottom), with carbon and hydrogen marked as reference points, to check vocabulary and ordering.
For a chosen metal, review its reaction with water and acid, its extraction method, and a short history note (gold found native, iron smelted, aluminium electrolytic).
Use the ladder as a lookup aid while doing the prediction and extraction tasks — not as the primary way to first learn the order.
activities.insight: A reference ladder consolidates vocabulary and the agreed order and links each position to extraction method and history.

checkQuestion: I drop a strip of magnesium into blue copper sulfate solution, and separately a strip of copper into colourless magnesium sulfate solution. In ONE of them a reaction happens and in the other nothing does. Which one reacts — and the important part, WHY that one and not the other?
checkAnswer: Only magnesium-in-copper-sulfate reacts: magnesium is MORE reactive than copper, so it displaces copper from the solution (blue fades, copper coats the strip). Copper-in-magnesium-sulfate does nothing because copper is LESS reactive than magnesium and can't displace it. The rule: a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one from its compound. Full marks turn on ordering by reactivity, not on which looks stronger/heavier.
